evals.prompt: We're running GoNorth in March - two rooms in a university building in Leeds, 14 talks across the day, about 260 people. It's our first edition. We want all the talks recorded and up on YouTube afterwards, no live stream. Budget is tight but not zero. I've got six volunteers who have never done AV before, and I found two secondhand camcorders plus a couple of tripods. Room A seats 180 and has a projector and a small PA with a mixing desk; Room B is a flat 80-seat seminar room with a TV on a trolley and no sound system at all. What do we actually need to buy and set up?
evals.expected_output: A production plan presented section by section for validation, stating the capture posture as recorded-for-later, picking a coverage tier per room, taking audio off the board in Room A, flagging Room B's missing sound system as an audio problem, drawing a three-destination signal path including a crew monitor, naming one production owner, choosing the full introduction training tier, and requiring a played-back test recording before doors.
expectations: States the capture posture explicitly as recorded for later, not streamed, before recommending any equipment
Chooses a coverage tier per room separately rather than applying one tier to the whole event
Specifies that the Room A recording takes its audio feed from the mixing board rather than from a camera's built-in microphone
Treats Room B's absence of a sound system as a problem for the recording's audio rather than assuming camera audio is acceptable there
Recommends a fixed camera taking the board feed as the default tier for at least one room rather than starting at multi-camera coverage
Describes a signal path with three destinations off one signal: the room's display, the recording or encoder path, and a monitor the crew watches
Identifies the crew monitor as the destination that catches a failure nobody would otherwise notice until editing
Names a single production owner and states that this person is not simultaneously MCing, speaking or running registration
Recommends the full introduction level of crew training rather than a brief refresher, on the grounds that this is a first edition with no experienced crew
Requires one test recording to be played back in full before the first session and distinguishes that from watching a level meter
Does not propose a smartphone as the capture plan for the 180-seat main room
Does not state a currency amount for any equipment item or crew cost
Presents the plan in sections for validation before anything is ordered

evals.prompt: A sponsor came back on our gold package and said they will only sign if we livestream the keynote. The event is in 19 days. We're a 300-person single-track community conference in Ghent, all volunteer. Our plan for the keynote right now is one camcorder on a tripod at the back recording to an SD card. Someone on the team said we can just put a laptop on the stream and point the camcorder's HDMI output at it, so it's basically free. Can we say yes to the sponsor?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to treat the unrehearsed, unstaffed laptop stream as a cheap tier of streaming, a statement of what a real stream requires (rehearsal plus a dedicated operator), the unanswered venue uplink question, the consent and music risks specific to live publication, and the technical cost reported back to the organizers so they take the commitment decision rather than the production layer taking it.
expectations: Refuses to treat the laptop plus camcorder arrangement as a cheaper tier of streaming and identifies it as the same cost with the failure built in
States that a livestream requires rehearsal arranged ahead of time and at least one person whose only job during the event is running it
Treats the absence of a dedicated stream operator as a blocker rather than a risk to accept
Does not recommend proceeding with the stream without both rehearsal and a dedicated operator
Reports what streaming adds technically and returns the decision on the sponsor commitment to the organizers instead of deciding the format itself
States that recording is the floor and streaming is the layer above it, so the existing recording plan is not sacrificed to fund the stream
Raises the venue's guaranteed upstream bandwidth as an open question that must be answered in writing
Does not state a specific megabits-per-second figure as this event's bandwidth requirement
Warns that on a live stream a speaker's opt-out has to be honoured in the room rather than in an edit
Warns that incidental or background music in a demo can get the stream taken down by the platform, and that speakers must be told before the day
Expresses any cost comparison between streamed or hybrid AV and physical-only AV as a ratio such as roughly double, never as a currency amount
Does not attribute a published conference loss or AV cost figure to a developer conference
Measures the 19 days against the last date the venue or a supplier can still add something, not against the event date alone

evals.prompt: Our contact at the Palais des Congres emailed asking us to send over 'your technical requirements' by Friday so they can price the rooms. We're a two-day, three-room developer conference, around 700 people, recording everything and streaming the main room. Can you draft what we send them? I was going to tell them we need 25 Mbps up and rigging for four cameras.
evals.expected_output: A venue technical specification written as questions the venue must answer in writing, covering connectivity with a guaranteed upstream figure, rigging, production space, power, house technician and recording or streaming restrictions, routed back through venue sourcing rather than sent as a direct negotiation.
expectations: Writes the venue document as questions the venue must answer in writing rather than as a specification of equipment or figures
Asks for the guaranteed upstream bandwidth to the streamed room and explicitly excludes the shared attendee figure and any best-effort number
Does not carry the user's 25 Mbps figure forward as the requirement stated to the venue
Asks whether a wired connection is available at the production position
Asks whether a second independent path to the internet exists
Asks who administers the venue network on the day and whether they are reachable during event hours
Asks where the rigging points are, what load they take, and who is permitted to rig
Asks whether a production position or control room is available in or adjacent to each room
Asks whether recording or streaming from the space is restricted by a house AV monopoly, an exclusivity clause or a fee
Asks whether an externally sourced AV supplier is permitted or whether the venue's nominated supplier must be used
Asks whether a house technician is included, for which hours, and what they are responsible for
Hands the document back through venue sourcing rather than opening a direct negotiation channel with the venue
Keeps the production uplink distinct from attendee internet provision rather than treating them as one requirement

evals.prompt: I've got quotes back from three AV companies for our conference - two rooms, two days, recording both rooms and streaming room 1. They're 11k, 17k and 26k euros, and the line items are so different I can't compare them. Write me the brief so I can pick one. The cheapest one said they'd 'record the talks in HD' and that is the entire video section of their quote.
evals.expected_output: An AV supplier brief structured so a supplier can price it line by line and delivery can be checked against it afterwards, including capture posture per room, coverage per room, a board-sourced audio requirement, recording deliverables with a naming convention and handover moment, required redundancy, a named organizer counterpart, and an acceptance criteria section - with the quote comparison and contracting handed to vendor sourcing rather than done here.
expectations: States that the technical brief belongs before supplier selection starts, and identifies quotes arriving first as the problem being described
Hands the quote comparison and the contracting decision to vendor sourcing rather than performing the comparison
Does not recommend one of the three suppliers or rank the three prices
States the capture posture per room explicitly in the brief, streamed for room 1 and recorded for room 2, rather than letting it be implied by the equipment list
Specifies coverage per room including camera count and whether each camera is operated or fixed
Includes an explicit requirement that the recording takes its audio from the mixing board rather than from a camera microphone
Specifies recording deliverables with format, resolution, frame rate, audio channels and a file naming convention
Specifies how and when files are handed over, naming a moment before the crew disperses rather than afterwards
Includes an acceptance criteria section defining how delivery will be judged, written before the event
Includes an acceptance criterion that every scheduled session has a playable file with audible board-sourced audio
Lists speaker-driven requirements such as live demos, audio playback, hardware props and non-standard connectors individually rather than summarising them as standard laptop connectivity
Names an organizer counterpart who owns the brief and checks delivery against it, alongside the supplier's own crew
States the required redundancy as a specified requirement in the brief rather than leaving the choice to the supplier

evals.prompt: Here's our backup plan for the conference, tell me if it's enough. We keep a spare mic and a spare camera in the AV cupboard at the back of the hall, and at the end of each day we copy everything off the SD cards onto the NAS in the office so there's a second copy. Last year we lost one talk because the recorder had stopped and nobody noticed, and I want to make sure that doesn't happen again. Two rooms, 22 sessions over two days, recorded not streamed.
evals.expected_output: A redundancy plan rebuilt against named failures, correcting the cupboard-stored spare mic, the end-of-day bulk copy and the duplicate camera, adding an independent audio-only second recording, a naming convention, clock sync, a crew monitor for the silent-failure case, one full test playback, and an owner plus a verification moment on every line.
expectations: Identifies that a spare microphone stored in a cupboard is not within reach of the position that needs it, and relocates it to the lectern with the room's audio owner
Identifies the end-of-day bulk copy as a network-load spike pattern and replaces it with copying between sessions or continuous chunked sync
States that the spare camera duplicates the layer least likely to fail silently, and does not treat a second camera as the primary redundancy
Recommends an independent second audio recording taken from the board but sitting outside the live mix
States that the independent second recording is audio-only, giving the reason that audio is what makes a recording usable
Requires a file naming convention applied to every recording device
Requires the clocks on every recording device to be set against one shared time reference
Requires one test playback of a real file before the event, played in full rather than checked as a level
Answers last year's stopped-recorder failure with a monitor on the record or encode output that somebody checks at the start of every session
Assigns a named owner to each redundancy element rather than listing techniques with no owner
States the specific failure each element protects against rather than describing redundancy in general terms
Treats a recording that exists but is unusable as a failure rather than a partial success
Does not recommend a full duplicate encoding chain as the first move for this event
Does not require an audio-over-IP transport or a large multi-track hardware recorder to reach the same principle

evals.prompt: Staffing question. Two rooms, one day. The main room gets two cameras because half the talks are code-heavy and one wide shot can't read the slides; the second room gets one fixed camera. I have four volunteers who have all helped at our last three editions, plus me. I was going to put one person on each camera, one floating, and me running everything else. Does that work?
evals.expected_output: A staffing correction that separates the camera operator from the vision mixer in the two-camera room, draws roles from the six-role menu without inventing empty roles, gives audio an explicit owner, flags the organizer running everything else, identifies the shortfall against the stated coverage, and picks the refresher-plus-hands-on training tier for a returning crew.
expectations: Separates the camera operator and the vision-mixing operator into two different people for the two-camera room
Identifies collapsing camera operation and vision mixing into one person as the specific error in the proposed staffing
Treats the named crew roles as a menu of jobs to draw from rather than a roster that must be fully filled
Does not assign a named role that has no work attached to it in this setup
Gives audio an explicit owner rather than leaving it inside the organizer's everything else
Flags the conflict if the organizer running everything else is also MCing, speaking or running registration
Recommends the brief refresher plus hands-on training tier rather than the full introduction, because the crew has returned across editions
States that newcomers still get the per-topic hands-on training even when the returning crew only needs the refresher
Concludes that the proposed five-person allocation is short for the stated coverage, or names exactly which position is unstaffed
Does not propose the venue's house technician as the owner of the recording, the files or the consent record
Distinguishes stage management from signal management rather than merging them into one job
Ties the second camera's value to slide legibility, matching the reason the user gave, rather than to production polish in general

evals.prompt: Our treasurer wants one number from me for the budget spreadsheet. She has a row called 'AV' and wants me to fill it in. We're recording two rooms, streaming the keynote, and the accessibility group said we need live captions in the main room. She also asked me to fold the attendee wifi into that number since it's all tech. What do I give her?
evals.expected_output: A Media cost line handed over already split into recording, captioning and live streaming, each with its own equipment, crew and supplier quote, with attendee internet and signage kept out as separate categories, and the shape of the line left to the budget owner.
expectations: Refuses to hand over a single lump AV number and hands over a split line instead
Splits the Media line into recording, captioning and live streaming as three separate parts
States that recording survives every tier down to the minimum and is therefore not the part cut first
States that live streaming is the first part a lean tier drops
States that dropping live streaming also drops the rehearsal and the dedicated operator attached to it
States that captioning's necessity was decided by accessibility and is delivered here rather than re-decided or traded away
Refuses to fold attendee wifi into the Media line and keeps attendee internet as its own category
Distinguishes the production pipeline's own uplink from attendee internet provisioning
Keeps signage out of the Media line as a separate category
Gives each of the three parts its own equipment, crew and supplier quote rather than one blended figure per part
States that the budget owner decides the shape of the line while production supplies its content
Does not invent a currency amount for any of the three parts

evals.prompt: A mess from last year that I want to avoid repeating. We recorded 19 talks, everyone went home, and the files sat on someone's laptop until March. We ended up publishing 11 of them and quietly dropped the rest because we couldn't remember which speakers had said yes to being recorded. This year's edition is in five months, same setup, 19 or 20 talks, one room, recorded not streamed. How do I set up the after-part so it doesn't happen again?
evals.expected_output: A post-event pipeline with a named owner and a date fixed before the event, file verification before the crew disperses, publication gated on the consent record collected upstream, per-speaker links, and self-set metrics including capture completeness that counts unusable recordings as failures.
expectations: Names an owner for the post-event pipeline and a publication date, both fixed before the event rather than after it
Requires every file to be verified as existing and playable before the crew disperses and leaves the building
Checks each recording against the consent record before publishing and marks anything the record does not cover as unpublishable
States that the consent record is collected upstream by speaker experience and consumed here rather than re-collected during editing
States that a camera being present in the room does not constitute a speaker's agreement to publication
Requires each speaker to be sent their own link once their talk is published
Counts a session that was recorded but is unusable as a failure in capture completeness rather than a partial success
Presents time from event end to published video as a number the organizers set for themselves rather than a published benchmark to hit
Identifies the point in the pipeline where it stalled and records it for the next edition
Does not propose retroactively chasing consent for last year's eight unpublished talks as the primary fix
Does not turn the answer into a clip, transcript or social repurposing plan for the recordings
Sets a pre-doors gate that every published-recording plan has a consent record covering that session's format

evals.prompt: We want to run a little podcast corner at our conference this year - pull speakers and a few attendees aside for 20-minute chats and release them as episodes afterwards. I was thinking we set up in a corner of the sponsor hall with one of those big mics on a boom between the two chairs, so it's visible and people wander over. Anything I'm missing?
evals.expected_output: On-site podcast recording treated as talk recording at smaller scale, with a genuinely quiet enclosed room, one microphone per participant, and per-participant written consent obtained before the first session, plus the same signal path, naming, test playback and redundancy discipline as the talk recordings.
expectations: Requires a genuinely quiet enclosed room rather than a corner of the sponsor hall
Requires one microphone per participant rather than a single shared microphone between the chairs
Requires written consent from each participant, obtained before the first session
States that the podcast's consent question differs from a talk's because a conversational recording captures people who never agreed to be on stage
Does not rely on the speaker consent record collected for stage talks to cover podcast guests
Applies the same signal path and redundancy approach used for talk recordings rather than treating the podcast as a separate discipline
Includes a second or independent audio capture, or an equivalent redundancy rung, for the podcast recordings
Requires a file naming convention and a test playback for the podcast recordings
Names an owner for the podcast recordings inside the production plan
Does not accept the sponsor hall's ambient noise as manageable with a directional microphone alone
Does not expand the answer into a standing podcast channel strategy, publishing cadence or between-edition guest pipeline

evals.prompt: We're streaming the opening keynote for the first time this year. I've blocked 45 minutes on the morning of the event for the AV team to test everything. What should they actually be doing in that 45 minutes? The room seats 400, two cameras, a vision mixer, a wireless handheld plus a headset for the speaker, house PA, and the venue gave us a wired drop at the production desk.
evals.expected_output: A rehearsal walkthrough run in the real room with the real equipment: the signal walked to all three destinations, a sixty-second recording played back in full, clocks and naming checked, a deliberate microphone failure timed with the person who would do it, one real transition at grid speed, a private live test watched from outside the venue network, and positions confirmed aloud by name.
expectations: Runs the rehearsal in the actual room with the actual equipment before the audience is in the building
Walks the signal end to end from microphone through the mixing position to each of the three destinations and confirms all three
Records sixty seconds and plays it back in full while listening, stating that a moving level meter is not evidence of a playable file
Checks the clock on every recording device against one shared reference
Confirms that the file naming convention produces the expected names
Breaks something deliberately, unplugging the primary microphone, and times the swap to the backup
Requires the person who would actually perform the swap on the day to be the one doing it in the drill, and treats the measured time as the honest measure of the redundancy
Runs one real transition at the changeover speed the schedule actually allows rather than at a relaxed pace
Goes live to a private destination and watches it on a device outside the venue network
States that a stream verified only from inside the building proves nothing about the uplink
Confirms out loud, by name, who is on which position for the first block
Treats rehearsal as a requirement for a livestream rather than a nicety, and does not offer to shorten or drop it if the morning runs late

evals.prompt: Seventh edition, three rooms, around 900 people over two days. We own four cameras, two recorders and a rack of cables, and eight people on the video crew have each done at least four editions. We record everything and stream the main room. Every year the videos take about four months to come out, and in one recent edition we lost a whole room's afternoon because a recorder filled up and nobody spotted it. I've got maybe 4k euros of headroom this year. Where should it go?
evals.expected_output: A re-ranked recommendation that says which stated fact moved which option, promotes continuous chunked sync to storage on the multi-room, recurring and prior-loss conditions, picks the refresher training tier, fixes the publication lag with a named owner and date, and answers the silent recorder failure with monitoring rather than more hardware.
expectations: Re-ranks the default menus against the owned equipment and the returning crew rather than presenting the default ordering unchanged
Names which stated fact moved which option, among the recurring editions, the owned equipment, the trained crew and the previous loss
Promotes continuous chunked sync to storage and cites the multi-room collection, the recurring event that amortises the setup, and the previous edition's lost recording
States that the ranking presented is a default rather than a law
Recommends the brief refresher plus hands-on training tier rather than a full introduction, given the returning crew
Treats the trained crew, the written brief and a repeatable pipeline as investments whose payoff lands after this edition, and promotes them because the event recurs
Answers the four-month publication lag by naming a pipeline owner and a date and identifying where the pipeline stalls
Answers the lost afternoon with a crew monitor and a per-block check rather than with additional recording hardware alone
Ranks the recommendation against the last date the venue or supplier can still add something rather than against the event date
Does not recommend a full duplicate encode path as the first use of the headroom
Does not recommend buying more cameras as the primary use of the headroom
Does not attach a currency amount to any individual recommendation
